title: Transient queueing probe diary — Ayla
content:
Goal: understand short-duration queueing effects when a small fraction (~1-3%) of requests are 4x longer (tokens) than median. Hypothesis: transient queuing + KV cache churn creates p99 spikes that don't show up in p95 or p50. Secondary: priority lanes (soft-priority) may hide the problem at low conc but amplify under mixed-priority fan-out.

Experiment topology:
- model: rw-infer/7b-optim (quantized), context max 1024, typical request length 40 tokens, long-tail at 160 tokens
- fleet: 4x gpus, multiplexing enabled, continuous batching with max-batch=128, batch-timeout=12ms
- arrival pattern: baseline poisson @ 120 qps, inject 1% "long" requests in 10s windows every 60s (simulate microburst)
- cache priming: warm, 95% hit expected; run both warm and cold-cache variants

Key knobs toggled across runs:
- preemptive-kv-eviction: on/off
- soft-priority lanes: enabled/disabled (2 lanes)
- batch-timeout: 6/12/24ms
- multiplexing slots per GPU: 4/8

Selected raw observations (aggregated from 3 runs each):
Run A (baseline): batch-timeout=12ms, kv-evict=on, multiplex=8
  qps(avg): 119.6, p50: 22ms, p95: 68ms, p99: 320ms
Run B (no preemptive eviction): batch-timeout=12ms, kv-evict=off
  qps(avg): 119.9, p50: 21ms, p95: 65ms, p99: 210ms  <-- p99 improved substantially
Run C (soft-priority enabled): p50: 20ms, p95: 64ms, p99: 410ms  <-- worse p99 tail, tail confined to low-priority lane
Run D (batch-timeout=6ms): throughput drops 3%, p99 increases to ~450ms (more small batches => higher scheduling overhead)

Notes/Interpretation:
- Biggest single win for p99 was disabling preemptive KV eviction. Looks like eviction during a microburst causes extra KV miss penalty leading to long-tail spikes. Might be because eviction runs a device-side copy or triggers slow path. Confirm by tracing KV eviction tasks + device timelines.
- Soft-priority hides spikes for high-priority traffic (p95 stays healthy) but low-priority requests see catastrophic p99s; when load increases, priority lane starves low tier and causes big tail amplification. For multi-tenant customers, policy needs to cap low-priority backlog or provide fallback model variant.
- Smaller batch-timeout increases variability; lower latency for median but scheduling jitter and more frequent kernel dispatch increases tail. There's a tradeoff curve; recommend adaptive batch-timeout that lengthens when backlog increases.

Quick checklist (next runs):
- Add high-fidelity tracing: correlate KV eviction timestamps with device memcpy and host-side GC events.
- Run eviction-only stress: continuous eviction every 5s at idle to reproduce penalty.
- Try TTL-based KV eviction (age-first) vs LRU to see interaction with typical request sequences.
- Test with cold-cache microburst (inject long request after 30s idle) to measure warmup penalty.
- Validate results on dedicated-capacity config (larger gpu pool) to see if multiplexing confounds results.

Questions for Jun/Luca:
- Do we have flamegraphs for device memcpy over time? I saw 2x memcpy spikes aligning with p99 windows but need confirmation.
- Any recent change to KV eviction code path since Oct that could explain device-side work?

Loose ideas for mitigation:
- Defer eviction work to background thread with strict IO-masking so it never runs during high qps windows.
- Make eviction incremental and cooperative with scheduler (slice eviction across batch boundaries).
- Implement soft QOS: when low-priority backlog grows > X, redirect to smaller model variant immediately.

To-dos (short):
- [ ] Upload full traces for Run A/B/C to S3: s3://redwood-bench/transient-queue/ayla_runs/ (pending)
- [ ] Open CAPA ticket for eviction tracing (JIRA-INF-790)
summary: Scratchpad: short-run probe of microburst-induced queueing + kv-cache eviction interactions. Initial finding: preemptive eviction causes notable p99 penalty; soft-priority lanes can amplify low-tier tails. Follow-up: add device traces and eviction-mode experiments.
